atoms.text: One of the moai is no longer on Easter Island, but is in London instead. This moai is called Hoa Hakananai'a.

trainers.instruction: Read the transcript of the following podcast to find out why and how Hoa Hakananai'a got to London.

atoms.b:
Dear listeners, welcome to another episode of my podcast Spaces in Places — the podcast focusing on art and culture around the world. Our guest this week is Professor Atamu from the ANTON University in London who specialises in Pacific Island Studies.
Today, we are going to talk about one of the most famous moai statues on Easter Island called Hoa Hakananai'a. As far as I know, it is the only moai that is not on Easter Island any more. Professor Atamu, how did that happen?

atoms.b: That is correct. In order to find out, we have to go back in time. The British ship Topaze, under the command of Commondore Powell, arrived at Rapa Nui island in 1868. At that time, Britain colonised many parts of the world, increasing their power over other peoples and lands.

At that time, Britain colonised many parts of the world, increasing their power over other peoples and lands. <break time='700ms'/>

atoms.b: So the British sailed all the way to this small remote island. What happened next?
atoms.sound: ssml: So the British sailed all the way to this small remote island. What happened next? <break time='700ms'/>

atoms.b: After discovering the island and its treasures, the crew wanted to bring back something beautiful to show their homeland. Upon seeing the moai, it was clear what that treasure would be. Eventually, they stumbled upon Hoa Hakananai'a standing upright in the back of a building. The statue was buried to its shoulders. The crew dug the statue out, hoisted it onboard the Topaze and shipped it to Britain. Today, Hoa Hakananai'a stands in the British Museum in London among many other objects.

atoms.b: On that note, it is important to remember that while some objects in the British Museum were gifted to Britain by indigenous peoples from across the world, many others were simply stolen and relocated to Britain without their consent. Many of these stolen objects are exhibited to this day.

atoms.b: That is very interesting! I have one last question, and I am sure our listeners are also curious: What does Hoa Hakananai'a mean?

atoms.b: Hoa Hakananai'a can be translated as 'stolen or hidden friend'. This name makes sense, since it is the only moai that is not on Easter Island anymore.
